content.html:
Module 8›Chapter 8.3›What is Azure Application Insights?

What is Azure Application Insights?

Your APM Solution for Live Web Applications

Core Definition

Azure Application Insights is an Application Performance Management (APM) service within Azure Monitor. It's designed to help you understand how your live web applications are performing by collecting rich telemetry data.

Why it Matters for DevOps

  • Provides deep, actionable insights into application health.
  • Identifies performance bottlenecks proactively.
  • Helps understand user behavior and interactions.
  • Enables true application-level observability beyond infrastructure.

How it Works

1. Instrumentation: Integrate SDKs into your application code.

2. Data Collection: Automatically gathers requests, dependencies, exceptions, and more.

3. Analysis: Sends telemetry to Azure for visualization and querying.

Key Takeaway

Application Insights is your essential tool for comprehensive APM, providing deep insights into your application's real-time performance and user experience.

screens.title: Tracking Application Flow
screens.narratorSegment: Application Insights automatically collects a wide array of standard telemetry, providing immediate visibility into your application's behavior. Two fundamental types are Requests and Dependencies. Requests capture detailed information about every incoming HTTP request to your web application. This includes the URL, the response time, whether the request succeeded or failed, and the HTTP response code. By analyzing request telemetry, you can quickly understand your application's overall throughput, identify slow endpoints, and monitor the success rate of user interactions. For instance, if you see a sudden spike in failed requests to a specific A P I endpoint, you know exactly where to investigate. On the other hand, Dependencies track all calls your application makes to external services. This could be a database query to Azure S Q L or Cosmos DB, an A P I call to another microservice, or even an external HTTP service. Dependency tracking is absolutely crucial for pinpointing bottlenecks that aren't within your application's code but rather in an external component it relies on. If a database query is consistently slow, Application Insights will highlight that dependency as the culprit, saving you valuable debugging time. Understanding these two telemetry types together gives you a powerful view of your application's internal and external interactions.

content.html:
Module 8›Chapter 8.3›Requests and Dependencies

Tracking Application Flow

Requests and Dependencies

Requests Telemetry

  • Captures incoming HTTP requests to your web app.
  • Includes URL, response time, success/failure status, response code.
  • Fundamental for understanding application throughput and latency.
  • Helps identify slow endpoints and user experience issues.
Example: A user loads a webpage, triggering an HTTP GET request to your server. Application Insights records its duration and status.
Key Takeaway

Requests provide insight into user-facing performance, while dependencies reveal external service bottlenecks.

Dependencies Telemetry

  • Tracks calls made by your application to external services.
  • Covers databases (SQL, Cosmos DB), other APIs, external HTTP services.
  • Crucial for identifying bottlenecks caused by slow external components.
  • Provides visibility into third-party service performance.
Example: Your application queries an Azure SQL Database. Application Insights tracks the query duration and success.
Pro Tip

Correlate requests and dependencies to trace an entire transaction flow and pinpoint exact performance culprits.

screens.title: Diagnosing Issues
screens.narratorSegment: Beyond requests and dependencies, Application Insights provides two more critical standard telemetry types for diagnosing issues: Exceptions and Traces. Exceptions are automatically recorded whenever an unhandled error occurs within your application. This telemetry is incredibly valuable because it provides not just the error message, but also the full stack trace, the type of exception, and contextual information about where and when the error occurred. Imagine a user reports an unexpected error; with exception telemetry, you can often pinpoint the exact line of code that failed, significantly accelerating your debugging process. Without this, you might be left guessing the root cause. Traces, also known as custom logs, allow you to send arbitrary log messages directly from your application code. These are invaluable for understanding the flow of execution through complex logic paths or for debugging specific features. You can log messages at different severity levels, such as information, warning, or error, and even attach custom properties to them. For example, you might log a trace message when a specific business rule is triggered or when a critical data transformation begins. This provides a breadcrumb trail through your application, helping you understand its internal workings and diagnose issues that might not manifest as full exceptions. Together, exceptions and traces give you a powerful toolkit for both reactive error handling and proactive diagnostic logging.

content.html:
Module 8›Chapter 8.3›Exceptions and Traces

Diagnosing Issues

Exceptions and Traces

Exceptions Telemetry

  • Records unhandled exceptions and errors in your application.
  • Provides stack traces, exception types, and contextual information.
  • Essential for debugging and understanding application failures.
  • Helps prioritize and fix critical bugs quickly.
Example: A database connection error causes an unhandled exception. Application Insights captures the full stack trace.
Key Takeaway

Exceptions provide immediate error context, while traces offer custom logging for detailed flow analysis.

Traces (Custom Logs)

  • Allows sending arbitrary log messages from application code.
  • Invaluable for understanding execution flow and debugging specific logic.
  • Supports different severity levels (Info, Warning, Error).
  • Can include custom properties for enhanced filtering.
Example: Log a message when a complex calculation starts or finishes, with relevant input parameters.
Common Mistake

Over-logging with traces can lead to high data volume and costs. Be selective and use appropriate severity levels.

screens.title: Instrumenting Your Application
screens.narratorSegment: To begin collecting all this valuable telemetry data, you first need to instrument your application. This process essentially involves integrating the Application Insights SDK into your application's codebase. Application Insights offers SDKs for a wide array of popular programming languages and frameworks, ensuring broad compatibility. Whether you're working with. NET, Java, Node. js, Python, or even client-side JavaScript, there's an SDK available to facilitate data collection. The instrumentation process typically starts with installing the appropriate SDK package for your environment. For instance, in a. NET application, you'd use a NuGet package, while in a Node. js project, you'd use an npm package. Once installed, the next crucial step is configuration. This usually involves providing an instrumentation key or, more securely and commonly now, a connection string. This unique identifier tells your application's SDK exactly which Application Insights resource in Azure to send its telemetry data to. Think of it as the address for your monitoring data. Without this configuration, your application wouldn't know where to send its performance and diagnostic information. Properly setting up this connection is the foundational step for unlocking all the powerful monitoring capabilities that Application Insights provides, ensuring your application's health is continuously observed.

content.html:
Module 8›Chapter 8.3›.NET Core Instrumentation

Instrumenting a .NET Core Web App

Step-by-Step SDK Integration

Installation & Configuration

  • Install NuGet Package: Add `Microsoft.ApplicationInsights.AspNetCore` to your project.
  • Configure Services: Use `builder.Services.AddApplicationInsightsTelemetry()` in `Program.cs`.
  • Connection String: Set `options.ConnectionString` from `appsettings.json` or environment variables.
  • Optional: Add custom `ITelemetryInitializer` for advanced scenarios.
Best Practice: Always use environment variables for connection strings in production to enhance security.
Key Takeaway

Properly adding the NuGet package and configuring the connection string in `Program.cs` is essential for .NET Core telemetry.

Program.cs.NET 6+
using Microsoft.ApplicationInsights.Extensibility;

var builder = WebApplication.CreateBuilder(args);

// Add Application Insights services
builder.Services.AddApplicationInsightsTelemetry(options =>
{
    // Configure with Connection String from appsettings.json or environment variables
    options.ConnectionString = builder.Configuration["APPLICATIONINSIGHTS_CONNECTION_STRING"];
});

// Optional: Configure custom telemetry processors or initializers
builder.Services.AddSingleton<ITelemetryInitializer, MyCustomTelemetryInitializer>();

// ... other services ...

var app = builder.Build();

// ... other middleware ...

app.Run();

content.html:
Module 8›Chapter 8.3›Node.js Instrumentation

Instrumenting a Node.js Application

SDK Setup and Basic Telemetry

Installation & Usage

  • Install npm Package: Use `npm install applicationinsights`.
  • Initialize SDK: Call `appInsights.setup(connectionString).start()`.
  • Default Client: Access `appInsights.defaultClient` for custom telemetry.
  • Track Methods: Use `trackEvent()`, `trackMetric()`, `trackTrace()` for custom data.
Remember to set `APPLICATIONINSIGHTS_CONNECTION_STRING` as an environment variable for secure deployment.
Key Takeaway

The Node.js SDK provides a straightforward way to initialize Application Insights and send various types of telemetry, including custom data.

app.jsNode.js
const appInsights = require('applicationinsights');

// Configure with Connection String
appInsights.setup(process.env.APPLICATIONINSIGHTS_CONNECTION_STRING)
    .setSendLiveMetrics(true) // Optional: Enable Live Metrics Stream
    .start();

const client = appInsights.defaultClient;

// Example: Track a custom event
client.trackEvent({ name: "UserLoggedIn", properties: { userId: "user123", method: "OAuth" } });

// Example: Track a custom metric
client.trackMetric({ name: "ItemsProcessed", value: 100 });

// Example: Log a trace message
client.trackTrace({ message: "Processing started for batch ABC", severity: appInsights.Contracts.SeverityLevel.Information });

// Your application logic here

screens.title: Capturing Business Logic
screens.narratorSegment: While standard telemetry provides an excellent baseline for application health, a key strength of Application Insights lies in its ability to implement custom events and metrics. This is where you can truly tailor your monitoring to capture application-specific business logic and unique user interactions. Standard telemetry tells you *if* a request was slow, but custom telemetry can tell you *why* a specific checkout flow failed or *how long* a critical calculation took. Custom events, tracked using Track Event open parenthesis close parenthesis, are perfect for recording discrete occurrences within your application. For instance, you might track when a user completes a specific checkout step, adds an item to their cart, or successfully registers for a service. You can attach custom properties to these events, providing rich context for later analysis. Custom metrics, on the other hand, tracked with Track Metric open parenthesis close parenthesis, are designed for numerical values. These could be the duration of a complex algorithm, the number of items processed in a batch, or the current queue size. By defining and tracking these custom data points, you gain significantly deeper insights into user behavior, the performance of critical business operations, and the overall effectiveness of your application from a business perspective. This granular data is invaluable for optimizing user experience and achieving specific business goals.

Module 8›Chapter 8.3›C# Custom Telemetry

Implementing Custom Telemetry in C#

Tracking Events, Metrics, and Traces

Using TelemetryClient

  • Inject `TelemetryClient`: Obtain an instance via dependency injection.
  • `TrackEvent()`: Record discrete actions with custom properties and metrics.
  • `TrackMetric()`: Capture numerical values for performance indicators.
  • `TrackTrace()`: Send structured log messages with severity levels.
Custom properties and metrics provide invaluable context for filtering and analysis in Application Insights.
Key Takeaway

The `TelemetryClient` in C# allows granular control over custom telemetry, enabling detailed monitoring of business logic and performance.

OrderService.csC#
public class OrderService
{
    private readonly TelemetryClient _telemetryClient;

    public OrderService(TelemetryClient telemetryClient)
    {
        _telemetryClient = telemetryClient;
    }

    public void ProcessOrder(string orderId, decimal amount)
    {
        // Track a custom event for order processing
        _telemetryClient.TrackEvent("OrderProcessed",
            new Dictionary<string, string> { { "OrderId", orderId }, { "User", "current_user" } },
            new Dictionary<string, double> { { "OrderAmount", (double)amount } });

        // Track a custom metric for order processing duration
        _telemetryClient.TrackMetric("OrderProcessingDurationMs", 150.0); // Example duration

        // Log a trace message
        _telemetryClient.TrackTrace("Order " + orderId + " successfully processed.",
            Microsoft.ApplicationInsights.DataContracts.SeverityLevel.Information);

        // ... actual order processing logic ...
    }
}

screens.title: Common Troubleshooting Scenarios
screens.narratorSegment: Even with careful instrumentation, you might encounter issues with Application Insights data collection. Knowing how to troubleshoot these common scenarios is a vital skill. One of the most frequent problems is an incorrect or missing instrumentation key or connection string. If this isn't configured correctly in your application's settings, no telemetry will be sent. Always double-check your application settings in Azure, ensuring the connection string is accurate and accessible to your application. Another common culprit is network connectivity issues or firewall rules. Your application needs outbound access on port 443 to the Application Insights ingestion endpoint, typically dc. services. visualstudio. com. For self-hosted agents or VMs, you might need to explicitly configure firewall rules. Sometimes, you might notice missing data points, which could be due to aggressive sampling. Application Insights can sample telemetry to reduce data volume and costs. You can adjust the sampling rate in your Application Insights configuration in the Azure portal if you need more granular data. Finally, a critical consideration is sensitive data. Avoid sending Personally Identifiable Information, or PII, or other confidential data in your custom events, metrics, or trace messages. Always implement proper data sanitization or redaction before sending telemetry to ensure compliance and security. Proactive troubleshooting ensures your monitoring remains robust.

Module 8›Chapter 8.3›Troubleshooting

Common Troubleshooting Scenarios

Diagnosing Application Insights Issues

Configuration & Connectivity

  • Incorrect Connection String: Verify `APPLICATIONINSIGHTS_CONNECTION_STRING` in app settings.
  • Network/Firewall Blocks: Ensure outbound access on port 443 to `dc.services.visualstudio.com`.
  • SDK Initialization: Confirm SDK is properly initialized and `TelemetryClient` is used.
Always check Azure App Service Configuration settings for correct environment variables.
Key Takeaway

Proactive troubleshooting of configuration, network, sampling, and data privacy ensures reliable Application Insights telemetry collection.

Data Collection & Privacy

  • Aggressive Sampling: Adjust sampling rate in Azure Portal if data points are missing.
  • Telemetry Processors: Review custom processors that might filter out data.
  • Sensitive Data (PII): Avoid sending PII; implement data sanitization/redaction.
  • High Data Volume: Optimize custom telemetry to balance insights with cost.
Never send sensitive user data directly to Application Insights without proper anonymization.
